misspelt.tip: two c's and two m's: it has room for both
the e of argue drops: argUment
i before e: never believe a lIE
double m, double t, double e
con-sci-ous: the sc sounds like sh
dis + appear: one s, two p's
dis + appoint: one s, two p's
fri-END: a friend to the end
two m's, keep the e: immediate + ly
keep the e after c so it stays soft
one f, one r in the middle
Rhythm Helps Your Two Hips Move
two c's, two s's, one l
sur-prise: don't drop the first r
tem-per-a-ture: four syllables when you spell it
two c's, one s, two l's
only one h in the middle
beau-ti-ful: one l at the end
Big Elephants Can Always Understand Small Elephants
two c's, two s's, two l's

rules.h: i before e, except after c
rules.body: Write ie when the sound is 'ee': believe, achieve, field, piece. After c write ei: receive, ceiling, deceive. Write ei when it sounds like 'ay': eight, weight, neighbour, vein.
ex: believe
receive
ceiling
piece
eight
rules.warn: Exceptions to learn by heart: weird, seize, either, neither, foreign, height, leisure, protein, science, species.

rules.body: Double the last consonant before -ed, -ing, -er when the word ends in one vowel + one consonant and the stress is on the last syllable: stop → stopped, begin → beginning, prefer → preferred, occur → occurred. If the stress is not on the last syllable, don't double: visit → visited, open → opening, happen → happened, benefit → benefited.
ex: stopped
beginning
preferred
occurred
visited
happened
rules.warn: British English always doubles a final l after a short vowel: travel → travelling, cancel → cancelled (American: traveling, canceled).

rules.body: Drop the final silent e before a suffix that starts with a vowel: make → making, write → writing, hope → hoping, use → usable. Keep it before a consonant suffix: hope → hopeful, use → useless, complete → completely, sincere → sincerely.
ex: writing
hoping
completely
hopeful
usable
rules.warn: Keep the e after c or g to keep the sound soft: noticeable, manageable, courageous. Exceptions: argument, truly, ninth, wholly.

rules.body: After a consonant, y changes to i before most suffixes: happy → happiness, carry → carried, study → studies, easy → easily. After a vowel, keep the y: play → played, enjoy → enjoyment.
ex: happiness
carried
studies
easily
played
rules.warn: Keep the y before -ing: studying, carrying, flying.

rules.body: If you can remove -able and still have a complete word, it's usually -able: accept → acceptable, depend → dependable, understand → understandable. If the root isn't a word on its own, it's often -ible: visible, possible, terrible, edible, horrible.
ex: acceptable
dependable
visible
possible
responsible
rules.warn: Learn the exceptions as you meet them: responsible, sensible, flexible (-ible), and probable, capable (-able).

rules.body: There is no reliable sound rule, but there are clues: words from verbs ending in -ere or -ist often take -ence: interfere → interference, exist → existence, insist → insistence. A hard c or g before the ending usually means a: significant, elegant; a soft c or g usually means e: innocent, intelligent.
ex: existence
interference
significant
intelligent
independent
rules.warn: Keep each family consistent: independent → independence, relevant → relevance, important → importance.

rules.body: Add -es after s, x, z, ch, sh: buses, boxes, churches, wishes. Consonant + y → -ies: city → cities. Many words in -f / -fe → -ves: knife → knives, life → lives, half → halves.
ex: churches
cities
knives
halves
boxes
rules.warn: Academic words keep their Latin or Greek plurals: criterion → criteria, phenomenon → phenomena, analysis → analyses, hypothesis → hypotheses.

rules.body: Many common words contain letters you don't hear: knife, write, debt, doubt, island, receipt, psychology, muscle, foreign, Wednesday, autumn, answer. Say them in your head as they are written ("Wed-nes-day") when you spell.
ex: receipt
psychology
muscle
autumn
answer

rules.body: British English allows both -ise and -ize (organise/organize); American English uses -ize. IELTS accepts either: just be consistent in one essay. Some words are always -ise: advertise, advise, compromise, exercise, surprise, supervise, televise.
ex: organise
recognise
advertise
surprise
exercise
rules.warn: Analyse (British) / analyze (American): always -yse in British English.

rules.body: When you add a prefix, just join it: dis + appear = disappear (one s), dis + satisfied = dissatisfied (two s's), mis + spell = misspell, un + necessary = unnecessary, ir + relevant = irrelevant, im + mature = immature.
ex: disappear
dissatisfied
misspell
unnecessary
irrelevant
rules.warn: Use im- before b, m, p (impossible, immature), il- before l (illegal), ir- before r (irregular).

rules.body: Choose one variety and stay consistent. British: colour, favour, centre, theatre, travelling, programme, defence, licence (noun), grey, catalogue. American: color, favor, center, theater, traveling, program, defense, license, gray, catalog.
ex: colour
centre
programme
defence
travelling
rules.warn: IELTS accepts both, but mixing them in one essay looks careless.

pairs.rule: affect = to influence (verb) · effect = a result (noun)
pairs.ex: Stress can affect your sleep. · The new law had a positive effect.

pairs.rule: their = belonging to them · there = in that place / there is
pairs.ex: Their car is over there.

pairs.rule: they're = they are · their = belonging to them
pairs.ex: They're bringing their children.

pairs.rule: its = belonging to it · it's = it is / it has
pairs.ex: It's clear the company has lost its way.

pairs.rule: your = belonging to you · you're = you are
pairs.ex: You're going to need your passport.

pairs.rule: then = after that, at that time · than = in comparisons
pairs.ex: It was bigger than I expected, and then it got worse.

pairs.rule: lose = fail to keep (verb) · loose = not tight (adjective)
pairs.ex: If the screw is loose, you'll lose it.

pairs.rule: accept = agree to receive · except = apart from
pairs.ex: I accept all the terms except the last one.

pairs.rule: advice = noun · advise = verb
pairs.ex: I advise you to take her advice.

pairs.rule: British: practice = noun, practise = verb
pairs.ex: I practise every day; practice makes perfect.

pairs.rule: British: licence = noun, license = verb
pairs.ex: You need a driving licence.

pairs.rule: principal = main; head of a school · principle = a rule or belief
pairs.ex: The principal reason is a matter of principle.

pairs.rule: stationary = not moving · stationery = paper, pens
pairs.ex: The car was stationary. We ordered new stationery.

pairs.rule: complement = complete or go well with · compliment = praise
pairs.ex: The wine complements the meal. She paid me a compliment.

pairs.rule: ensure = make certain · insure = buy insurance for
pairs.ex: Ensure the house is insured.

pairs.rule: economic = relating to the economy · economical = saving money
pairs.ex: Economic growth slowed. Small cars are more economical.

pairs.rule: historic = important in history · historical = connected with the past
pairs.ex: A historic victory. Historical records.

pairs.rule: sensible = showing good judgement · sensitive = easily affected / aware of feelings
pairs.ex: A sensible decision. Sensitive skin.

pairs.rule: raise = lift something (takes an object) · rise = go up (no object)
pairs.ex: They raised prices, so costs rose.

pairs.rule: lay = put something down (laid, laid) · lie = be in a flat position (lay, lain)
pairs.ex: Lay the book on the table and lie down.

pairs.rule: borrow = take for a while · lend = give for a while
pairs.ex: Can I borrow your pen? Can you lend me your pen?

pairs.rule: fewer + countable · less + uncountable
pairs.ex: Fewer cars mean less traffic.

pairs.rule: between = two (or clearly separate) things · among = a group
pairs.ex: Between you and me, the money was shared among the staff.

pairs.rule: the speaker implies · the listener infers
pairs.ex: She implied I was late; I inferred she was annoyed.

pairs.rule: continual = repeated, with breaks · continuous = without stopping
pairs.ex: Continual interruptions. A continuous line.

pairs.rule: discreet = careful not to attract attention · discrete = separate
pairs.ex: Please be discreet. Three discrete stages.

pairs.rule: council = a group that governs · counsel = advice / to advise
pairs.ex: The city council sought legal counsel.

pairs.rule: desert = dry land / to abandon · dessert = sweet course (two s's: you want more)
pairs.ex: We had dessert in the desert.

pairs.rule: weather = rain, sun · whether = if
pairs.ex: I don't know whether the weather will change.

pairs.rule: quite = fairly · quiet = silent
pairs.ex: It was quite quiet.

pairs.rule: thorough = complete, careful · through = from one side to the other
pairs.ex: A thorough search through the files.

pairs.rule: adapt = change to fit · adopt = take as your own
pairs.ex: We adopted the policy and adapted it to local needs.

pairs.rule: elicit = draw out (a response) · illicit = illegal
pairs.ex: The question elicited a laugh. Illicit drugs.

pairs.rule: eminent = famous, respected · imminent = about to happen
pairs.ex: An eminent scientist warned of an imminent crisis.

pairs.rule: personal = private, individual · personnel = staff
pairs.ex: Personnel files contain personal data.

pairs.rule: moral = right and wrong · morale = confidence, spirit of a group
pairs.ex: Team morale was low.

pairs.rule: site = place · sight = ability to see / something seen
pairs.ex: The building site was an ugly sight.

pairs.rule: cite = quote as evidence · site = place
pairs.ex: Cite three sources.

pairs.rule: alternate = every other / take turns · alternative = another option
pairs.ex: We meet on alternate Mondays. Is there an alternative?

pairs.rule: especially = particularly · specially = for a special purpose
pairs.ex: Especially in winter. Specially designed for children.

pairs.rule: see lose / loose
pairs.ex: Don't lose your loose change.

pairs.rule: British: dependant = a person (noun) · dependent = adjective
pairs.ex: He is dependent on his parents; they have two dependants.

pairs.rule: everyday = ordinary (adjective) · every day = each day
pairs.ex: Everyday problems happen every day.

pairs.rule: maybe = perhaps · may be = might be
pairs.ex: Maybe he's right. He may be right.

pairs.rule: who's = who is · whose = belonging to whom
pairs.ex: Who's the man whose car is outside?

pairs.rule: passed = verb (pass) · past = time before / beyond
pairs.ex: She passed the exam. In the past.

pairs.rule: breath = noun · breathe = verb
pairs.ex: Take a deep breath and breathe slowly.

pairs.rule: cloth = material · clothes = what you wear · clothe = to dress
pairs.ex: Cotton cloth. Food and clothes.

task1.title: Line graph: public transport use
task1.prompt: The graph below shows the average number of journeys per person per year made by bus, train and bicycle in a European city between 2000 and 2020. Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparisons where relevant.

task1.title: Bar chart: how students spend their time
task1.prompt: The chart below shows the average number of hours per week that university students in three countries spent on studying, paid work and leisure in 2023. Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparisons where relevant.

task1.title: Table: household energy use
task1.prompt: The table below shows the percentage of household energy used for different purposes in two countries in 1990 and 2020. Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparisons where relevant.

task1.title: Process: recycling glass bottles
task1.prompt: The diagram below shows how glass bottles are recycled. Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features.

steps: Bottles collected from homes and bottle banks
Melted in a furnace at about 1,500°C
Filled, labelled and sent to shops

task2.prompt: Some people believe that unpaid community service should be a compulsory part of high school programmes. To what extent do you agree or disagree?

Some people think that governments should invest more in public transport, while others believe that building more roads is the better solution to traffic problems. Discuss both views and give your own opinion.
More and more people are choosing to work from home rather than in an office. Do the advantages of this development outweigh the disadvantages?
In many cities, young people find it increasingly difficult to afford a place to live. What are the causes of this problem, and what measures could be taken to solve it?
Many people today rely on social media as their main source of news. Why is this the case? Is this a positive or negative development?
Artificial intelligence will soon make many university degrees unnecessary. To what extent do you agree or disagree?
Some people argue that museums and art galleries should be free for everyone, while others think visitors should pay. Discuss both views and give your opinion.
In some countries, a growing number of students study abroad for their university degree. What are the advantages and disadvantages of this trend?

check1: Paraphrased the question in the first sentence (didn't copy it)
Wrote a clear overview of the main trends or the biggest differences (no numbers needed there)
Grouped information logically in 2 body paragraphs
Supported key points with accurate figures and dates
Made comparisons (higher than, twice as many, while, whereas)
Used a range of trend vocabulary (rose steadily, peaked at, fell sharply, remained stable)
Did NOT give opinions or reasons that aren't in the chart
Wrote at least 150 words in about 20 minutes
Checked tenses (past for past data, future forms for projections)
Checked spelling of the key words I used most
check2: Answered every part of the question
My position is clear in the introduction and the conclusion
Each body paragraph has one main idea with a clear topic sentence
Each idea is explained and supported with a reason or an example
Used linking words naturally (not at the start of every sentence)
Used pronouns and synonyms to avoid repeating the same nouns
Used less common vocabulary and collocations accurately
Mixed simple and complex sentences (relative clauses, conditionals, passives)
Wrote at least 250 words in about 40 minutes
Proofread: articles, plurals, subject–verb agreement and spelling

d: Fully answers every part; position is clear and fully developed throughout (T2) / an excellent overview with all key features (T1).
Organisation is effortless; linking never draws attention to itself; paragraphing is skilful.
Wide, natural and precise vocabulary; errors are very rare 'slips'.
Wide range of structures used with full flexibility; errors are rare slips.
Answers all parts well; ideas are relevant, extended and well supported.
Information is sequenced logically; cohesion is managed well; paragraphing is sufficient and appropriate.
Wide vocabulary used fluently to convey precise meaning; uncommon words used skilfully, with occasional inaccuracy in word choice or collocation.
Wide range of structures; most sentences are error-free; only occasional errors.
Addresses all parts; a clear position throughout; main ideas extended and supported, though some may be over-generalised (T2) / a clear overview of main trends (T1).
Logical organisation with clear progression; a range of linking devices, with some under- or over-use.
Enough range for flexibility and precision; some less common words and awareness of style and collocation; occasional errors in word choice or spelling.
A variety of complex structures; frequent error-free sentences; good control, with a few errors.
Addresses all parts, though some more fully than others; position is relevant but conclusions may be unclear or repetitive; some ideas lack development.
Organised coherently with overall progression; linking is effective but may be faulty or mechanical; paragraphing not always logical.
Adequate range for the task; attempts less common vocabulary with some inaccuracy; some spelling and word-formation errors that don't block meaning.
A mix of simple and complex forms; some errors in grammar and punctuation, but they rarely reduce communication.
Only partly addresses the task; position is unclear; main ideas are limited and not sufficiently developed; may include irrelevant detail.
Some organisation, but a lack of overall progression; inadequate, inaccurate or over-used linking; repetitive.
Limited range, minimally adequate; noticeable spelling and word-formation errors that may cause difficulty for the reader.
A limited range of structures; complex sentences are attempted but tend to be less accurate; frequent errors.

grammar.body: After a negative or limiting adverbial at the start of a sentence, use question word order (auxiliary + subject). It sounds formal and emphatic.
ex: Never have I seen such a mess.
Not only did she pass, but she also came top of the class.
Rarely do we get a chance like this.
Only after the meeting did I realise my mistake.
No sooner had we arrived than it started to rain.
Under no circumstances should you open this door.
q: I had never been so nervous. (Never …)
Never had I been so nervous.
He not only lost the match, he also injured his knee. (Not only …)
Not only did he lose the match, but he also injured his knee.
We only understood the risk later. (Only later …)
Only later did we understand the risk.
As soon as I sat down, the phone rang. (No sooner …)
No sooner had I sat down than the phone rang.

grammar.body: Split one sentence into two parts to focus on one element. It is/was … that/who … focuses on a noun or phrase; What … is/was … focuses on an action or idea; All (that) … is … means 'the only thing'.
ex: It was Sara who found the error, not me.
It's the noise that I can't stand.
What annoys me is the lack of communication.
What we need is a clear plan.
All I want is a quiet weekend.
The reason why I called is to apologise.
q: The price surprised me. (What …)
What surprised me was the price.
Tom broke the window. (It was …)
It was Tom who broke the window.
I only need ten minutes. (All …)
All I need is ten minutes.
She needs more practice. (What she …)
What she needs is more practice.

grammar.body: Mix the time frames when a past condition has a present result, or a present situation would have changed a past result. Past → present: If + past perfect, would + infinitive. Present → past: If + past simple, would have + past participle.
ex: If I had taken that job, I would be living in Dubai now.
If she hadn't missed the train, she would be here by now.
If I spoke Russian, I would have understood the film.
If he weren't so stubborn, he would have apologised.
q: I didn't study medicine, so I'm not a doctor now. (If …)
If I had studied medicine, I would be a doctor now.
I'm not tall, so I didn't get into the basketball team. (If …)
If I were taller, I would have got into the basketball team.
We didn't book, so we have nowhere to sit. (If …)
If we had booked, we would have somewhere to sit.

grammar.body: Replace a clause with an -ing or past participle to make writing shorter and more formal. The subject of both clauses must be the same. Having + past participle shows the first action finished before the second.
ex: Walking home, I saw an old friend. (= While I was walking)
Having finished the report, she went home.
Built in 1890, the bridge is still in use.
Not knowing what to say, he stayed silent.
The man standing at the door is my uncle.
q: After he had read the letter, he tore it up. (Having …)
Having read the letter, he tore it up.
Because I didn't want to be late, I took a taxi. (Not …)
Not wanting to be late, I took a taxi.
The house, which was designed by a famous architect, is now a museum. (Designed …)
Designed by a famous architect, the house is now a museum.

grammar.body: Academic writing often turns verbs and adjectives into nouns. This lets you pack more information into a sentence and sound more objective: Prices increased rapidly → There was a rapid increase in prices.
ex: The government decided to … → The government's decision to …
Unemployment rose sharply. → There was a sharp rise in unemployment.
People are becoming more aware of … → There is growing awareness of …
Because the company failed … → The failure of the company …
q: Sales fell dramatically in 2020. (There was …)
There was a dramatic fall in sales in 2020.
The city expanded quickly, which caused problems. (The rapid …)
The rapid expansion of the city caused problems.
Scientists discovered the virus, which changed medicine. (The discovery …)
The discovery of the virus changed medicine.

grammar.body: In academic and IELTS writing, avoid over-strong claims. Use modal verbs (may, might, could), verbs (appear, seem, tend, suggest), adverbs (possibly, arguably, largely) and phrases (to some extent, in most cases).
ex: Social media causes depression. → Heavy social media use may contribute to depression.
This proves that … → This suggests that …
Everyone agrees … → It is widely accepted that …
It is arguably the most important factor.
q: Video games make children violent. (hedge it)
Some violent video games may make some children more aggressive.
This shows the policy failed. (hedge it)
This appears to suggest that the policy was largely unsuccessful.

grammar.body: Use reporting passives to sound impersonal: It is said/believed/thought that … or Subject + is said/believed + to + infinitive (to have + past participle for the past). Also have/get something done.
ex: It is believed that the painting is a fake.
The painting is believed to be a fake.
He is thought to have left the country.
The company is reported to be losing money.
We're having the kitchen redone.
q: People say that he is a millionaire. (He is said …)
He is said to be a millionaire.
People believe the fire started in the kitchen. (The fire is …)
The fire is believed to have started in the kitchen.
Someone is repairing my car. (I'm having …)
I'm having my car repaired.

grammar.body: After verbs and adjectives of demand or importance, formal English uses the base form for all persons: insist/recommend/suggest/essential that he be / go. After wish, if only, it's (high) time, would rather, use a past form for the present.
ex: The committee recommended that she be promoted.
It is essential that every student attend the meeting.
I'd rather you didn't tell anyone.
It's high time we left.
If only I had more time.
q: The doctor said he must rest. (The doctor insisted that he …)
The doctor insisted that he rest.
We should go now. (It's time …)
It's time we went.
Please don't smoke here. (I'd rather you …)
I'd rather you didn't smoke here.

grammar.body: Fluent speakers leave out or replace words that are already clear: so / not (I think so / I hope not), do so, one / ones, and leaving out a verb after an auxiliary (She can swim but I can't).
ex: 'Will it rain?' 'I hope not.'
He promised to help and he did so.
I wanted the red one, not the blue one.
She's been to Japan, but I haven't.
I'd like to come, but I'm not sure I'll be able to.
q: 'Is the shop open?' 'I think that it is open.' (shorten)
'Is the shop open?' 'I think so.'
He said he would call and he called. (do so)
He said he would call and he did so.

grammar.body: Move information to the front for emphasis or to link with the previous sentence (Gone are the days when …, Such was the demand that …, So severe was the storm that …). Build long noun phrases with pre- and post-modifiers instead of several short sentences.
ex: Gone are the days when a degree guaranteed a job.
Such was the demand that tickets sold out in minutes.
So severe was the storm that the airport closed.
A recently published government report on youth unemployment in coastal towns …
q: The storm was so strong that trees fell. (So strong …)
So strong was the storm that trees fell.
The demand was so great that the site crashed. (Such …)
Such was the demand that the site crashed.

grammar.body: Know the grammar of each linker. Although / even though / whereas / while + clause. Despite / in spite of + noun or -ing. However / nevertheless / nonetheless start a new sentence (with a comma). Albeit + adjective or phrase (formal).
ex: Although it was expensive, we bought it.
Despite the cost, we bought it. / Despite being expensive, …
It was expensive. Nevertheless, we bought it.
The results were positive, albeit limited.
Some prefer cities, whereas others prefer the countryside.
q: It rained, but we played. (Despite …)
Despite the rain, we played.
He is rich, but he is unhappy. (Although …)
Although he is rich, he is unhappy.
The plan was successful but expensive. (albeit)
The plan was successful, albeit expensive.

grammar.t: Future in the past & advanced tenses
grammar.body: Talk about the future as seen from the past with was going to, was about to, was to (have), would. Use future continuous and future perfect for precise time reference: will be doing, will have done, will have been doing.
ex: I was going to call you, but I forgot.
We were about to leave when she arrived.
He was to become the youngest prime minister in history.
This time next year I'll be studying in London.
By 2030, the city will have doubled in size.
q: I planned to email you, but my laptop broke. (I was going …)
I was going to email you, but my laptop broke.
The project ends before June. (By June, the project …)
By June, the project will have ended.

grammar.body: Every English verb form combines three choices. Time: past, present or future. Aspect: simple (a complete fact or habit), continuous (in progress, temporary, unfinished) or perfect (connected to a later time). Voice: active or passive. Choose the aspect for the meaning you want, not because of a 'signal word'.
ex: I've lived here for three years. (still true now)
I lived there for three years. (finished)
She's been working too hard lately. (recent, ongoing activity)
The bridge was being repaired when we arrived. (passive, in progress)
By the time you read this, I'll have left.
The results have just been published.
q: They are building a new school. (passive)
A new school is being built.
I started learning English six years ago and I still learn it. (present perfect continuous)
I have been learning English for six years.
When I arrived, the film started already. (correct the tense)
When I arrived, the film had already started.

grammar.body: Some adverbs have two forms with different meanings: hard / hardly, late / lately, near / nearly, high / highly, free / freely. Strong adverbs go with strong adjectives (absolutely exhausted, not very exhausted). Opinion adjectives come before fact adjectives, usually in the order: opinion – size – age – shape – colour – origin – material – purpose.
ex: He works hard, but he hardly ever takes a break.
I haven't seen her lately; she arrived late again.
It's highly unlikely. The plane flew high above the clouds.
I was absolutely furious. / I was very angry.
a lovely little old wooden house
an expensive new Italian leather sofa
q: I was very exhausted. (correct it)
I was absolutely exhausted.
a wooden old beautiful table (correct the order)
a beautiful old wooden table
I've been very busy late. (correct it)
I've been very busy lately.

grammar.body: Some verbs take to + infinitive (decide, refuse, manage, afford), some take -ing (avoid, enjoy, keep, mind, consider), and some take both with a change of meaning: remember/forget/regret/stop/try/go on. With remember, forget, regret: -ing looks back at the past, to-infinitive looks forward to a duty.
ex: I stopped smoking. (I gave up) / I stopped to smoke. (in order to)
Remember to lock the door. / I remember locking the door.
Try turning it off and on again. (an experiment) / I tried to lift it. (difficult)
We regret to inform you … / I regret saying that.
She went on talking. / She went on to become a doctor.
Prices keep improving? No: Things keep getting better.
q: I'll never forget the day I met you. (use 'meeting')
I'll never forget meeting you.
Don't forget: post the letter. (Don't forget …)
Don't forget to post the letter.
He was talking and didn't stop. (He went on …)
He went on talking.

grammar.body: Show how sure you are with modals. Present: must / might / may / could / can't + infinitive (or + be + -ing). Past: must / might / may / could / can't / couldn't + have + past participle. Use should have / shouldn't have to criticise a past action, and needn't have for something done that wasn't necessary.
ex: She must be at home: the lights are on.
He can't be serious!
They might be waiting at the station.
You must have been exhausted after the flight.
She can't have seen us; she didn't wave.
You shouldn't have told him. / I needn't have brought an umbrella.
q: I'm sure he forgot. (must)
He must have forgotten.
It's impossible that she said that. (can't)
She can't have said that.
It was a mistake to buy it. (shouldn't)
I shouldn't have bought it.

grammar.body: Defining clauses identify which person or thing (no commas; that is possible; the pronoun can be left out when it is the object). Non-defining clauses add extra information (commas; never that; never left out). Which can refer to a whole clause. Formal English puts prepositions before whom/which.
ex: The man (who/that) I met was a doctor.
My brother, who lives in Canada, is a doctor.
He failed the exam, which surprised everyone.
The person to whom I spoke was very helpful.
That's the town where I grew up.
The reason why I'm calling is …
q: My sister lives in Riga. She is a teacher. (non-defining)
My sister, who lives in Riga, is a teacher.
He didn't call me. That annoyed me. (which)
He didn't call me, which annoyed me.
The woman I spoke to was helpful. (formal, with whom)
The woman to whom I spoke was helpful.

grammar.body: Discourse markers show how ideas connect and how you feel about them. Attitude: honestly, frankly, admittedly, surprisingly, unfortunately, obviously. Contrast or limit: mind you, still, all the same, even so. Giving a reason: after all. Changing topic: anyway, by the way, as for … Summing up: basically, in short.
ex: Frankly, I think it's a waste of money.
It's expensive. Mind you, it is very good quality.
Don't be too hard on him. After all, he's only six.
Anyway, that's enough about me.
Admittedly, I didn't try very hard.
It rained all week. Still, we had a good time.
q: Add a marker that limits the point: 'The hotel was noisy. ___, the staff were lovely.'
Mind you / Still / Even so, the staff were lovely.
Add a marker giving a reason: 'Let him go. ___, it's his birthday.'
After all, it's his birthday.

task3.title: A personal profile
task3.prompt: Write a personal profile of yourself for a student exchange website (200–250 words). Include your background, what you study, what you are like as a person and what you hope to get out of the exchange.

task3.title: A short story
task3.prompt: Write a short story (250–300 words) that begins with the sentence: 'Nobody noticed when the lights went out.' Use a variety of past tenses and some carefully chosen adjectives and adverbs.

task3.title: A report using a graph
task3.prompt: Write a short report (200–250 words) on how the population of your home city has changed over the last 30 years. Describe the main trends using language such as 'rose sharply' and 'levelled off', and suggest one reason for each change.

task3.title: A formal email of apology
task3.prompt: You booked a meeting room at your university but did not use it and did not cancel, so another group could not use it. Write a formal email to the administrator (150–200 words) apologising, explaining what happened and saying what you will do in future.

task3.title: Comparing two countries
task3.prompt: Write an essay (250–300 words) comparing everyday life in two countries you know well, for example Libya and Latvia: food, family life, attitudes to time and the weather. Use whereas, while, unlike, similarly and both … and.

task3.title: A short talk on a period in history
task3.prompt: Prepare the text of a three-minute talk (300 words) about a period in your country's history that changed people's lives. Use emphatic structures (What surprised me most was …, It was … that …) to make it easy to listen to.

task3.title: A letter to your younger self
task3.prompt: Write an informal letter (200–250 words) to yourself at age 13. Tell your younger self what you wish you had known, using mixed conditionals (If I had known …, I would be …) and 'would'.

task3.title: A folk tale with style
task3.prompt: Retell a folk tale or fable from your culture (250–300 words). Use relative clauses and participle clauses to join ideas and avoid short, choppy sentences.

task3.title: An opinion post
task3.prompt: Write a post (150–200 words) for an online discussion: 'Should schools spend more time on music and art?' Give your opinion informally, using attitude adverbs and discourse markers (honestly, mind you, after all).

task3.title: An opinion piece
task3.prompt: Write an opinion piece (250–300 words) for a student magazine: 'Doctors should be allowed to prescribe placebos.' Present both sides, use distancing language (It is said that …, appears to …) and give your own view.

task3.title: An online product review
task3.prompt: Write an online review (200 words) of a piece of technology you own: describe it, evaluate what is good and bad about it, and say who you would recommend it to.

task3.title: A short biography
task3.prompt: Write a short biography (250 words) of someone who has influenced you. Connect your ideas with linking devices (furthermore, meanwhile, nevertheless, as a result) and describe a turning point in their life.

headway.focus: Tense review (active/passive, simple/continuous, perfect/non-perfect); reflexive pronouns
Adverbs and adjectives, adverb collocations, adverbs with two forms, adjective order
Verb patterns (infinitive and -ing); describing trends; phrasal verbs with up and down
Modal verbs for speculation (present and past) and their other meanings
Ways to avoid repetition: missing words out, reduced infinitives, synonyms; British and American English
Ways of adding emphasis: cleft sentences, negative inversion, emphatic do/does/did; nouns from phrasal verbs
Real and unreal tenses: mixed conditionals, uses of would; phrasal verbs with on and off
Relative clauses and participles; homonyms, homophones and homographs
Discourse markers: attitude adverbs and connectors; verb phrases; rhyme and rhythm
Distancing the facts: passive reporting, seem and appear; compound nouns; words for the body
Future forms and future in the past; synonyms and antonyms
Linking devices (thus, furthermore, meanwhile, nevertheless); emphatic do/does/did; metaphorical language
